precepts.text: We know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. We all go through things we don't understand while we're going through them. Whether you're suffering poverty, health problems, eviction, trials, or temptations, endure to the end; there's a purpose.

He may not have understood it while he was in the midst of it, but going through the years of plenty and famine he realized his purpose, and God set that whole thing up.

note.label: Joseph in Egypt: Then & Now

precepts.why:
When Jacob died, Joseph's brethren were afraid: “Joseph will peradventure hate us, and will certainly requite us all the evil which we did unto him.” They sent a messenger begging forgiveness, “And Joseph wept when they spake unto him.” Then he said, “Fear not: for am I in the place of God?” “But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.”

Only a spiritual man can understand that. Joseph was on another level of understanding. He sat back and reflected on everything that happened to him, the pit, the slavery, the lie, the dungeon, and knew it was God's divine plan. He may not have understood it while he was in the midst of it, but going through the seven years of plenty and the seven years of famine he realized his purpose. God set that whole thing up.

Paul gives the precept: “And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.” We all go through things we don't understand while we are going through them, asking why God is doing this to me and nobody else. There is a purpose.

All things means all things: poverty, health problems, eviction, trials, tribulations, temptations, whatever it is. If you love God, you must endure it to the end, as Joseph did, and it will work together for good.

precepts.text: The Lord turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends; the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before, and blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning. Endure to the end and God shall restore everything.
precepts.point: Only a spiritual man can understand that. Joseph was on another level of understanding: he sat back and reflected on all that happened to him and knew it was God's divine plan. He may not have understood it while he was in the midst of it, but going through the years of plenty and famine he realized his purpose, and God set that whole thing up.

note.label: Joseph in Egypt: Then & Now

precepts.why:
Endure to the end, and God shall restore everything. Job is the proof: “And the Lord turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends: also the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before.”

His brethren and sisters and old acquaintances came and ate bread with him, “and they bemoaned him, and comforted him over all the evil that the Lord had brought upon him.” “So the Lord blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning: for he had fourteen thousand sheep, and six thousand camels, and a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she asses.” He had seven sons and three daughters, Jemima, Kezia and Keren-happuch, “And in all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job.”

Joseph's life ran the same way: sold, slandered, imprisoned, and then made ruler over Egypt, with his brethren falling down before his face. The latter end was greater than the beginning. Whatever you are suffering, endure it; God turns the captivity of those who hold on, and blesses their latter end more than their beginning.

precepts.text: Ye that fear the Lord, wait for his mercy, and go not aside, lest ye fall. Believe him, and your reward shall not fail. Look at the generations of old, and see: did ever any trust in the Lord, and was confounded? Was Job confounded? No. For the Lord is full of compassion and mercy, and saveth in time of affliction.
precepts.point: Only a spiritual man can understand that. Joseph was on another level of understanding: he sat back and reflected on all that happened to him and knew it was God's divine plan. He may not have understood it while he was in the midst of it, but going through the years of plenty and famine he realized his purpose, and God set that whole thing up.

note.label: Joseph in Egypt: Then & Now

precepts.why:
Sirach speaks to those in the middle of the trial: “Ye that fear the Lord, wait for his mercy; and go not aside, lest ye fall.” Don't go aside; don't say, I want to leave this truth and do something else. If you do, you will fall.

“Ye that fear the Lord, believe him; and your reward shall not fail.” “Ye that fear the Lord, hope for good, and for everlasting joy and mercy.”

“Look at the generations of old, and see; did ever any trust in the Lord, and was confounded? or did any abide in his fear, and was forsaken?” Was Job confounded? No. Was Joseph forsaken? No; what his brethren meant for evil, God meant for good. “For the Lord is full of compassion and mercy, longsuffering, and very pitiful, and forgiveth sins, and saveth in time of affliction.”

That is the close of Joseph's story: wait on the Lord, go not aside, and he saves in the time of affliction.

precepts.text: Ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good, to save much people alive.
precepts.point: The Midianites sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.

note.label: Genesis 37: Joseph the Dreamer

precepts.why:
Joseph told his brethren later what was really behind it all: “But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.” The brothers meant evil when they sold him and dipped his coat in blood; God meant it unto good.

That is why Jacob could not see through the lie. The thing was of the Lord. Had Joseph never gone down to Egypt, the whole house of Israel would have died in the famine. So the Midianites selling him “into Egypt unto Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh’s, and captain of the guard” was God sending him ahead to save much people alive.

precepts.text: The Canaanites saw the mourning and said, this is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians; the twelve tribes were mistaken for Egyptians.
precepts.point: And Joseph remembered the dreams which he dreamed of them. The sheaves that made obeisance to his sheaf were now his brethren bowing down themselves before him with their faces to the earth.

note.label: Genesis 42: Joseph's Brethren Bow Down in Egypt

precepts.why:
When Jacob died and his sons carried him up to bury him, they mourned at the threshingfloor of Atad, and “when the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning in the floor of Atad, they said, This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians.” The Canaanites saw the twelve tribes and took them all for Egyptians. Israel is black as night, just like the ancient Egyptians; all twelve tribes looked like the people of Egypt.

That is one reason Joseph’s brethren knew him not. He blended in among the Egyptians. Time had passed, they supposed he was dead or a slave, and they never expected their brother to be second in command over Egypt; and standing before them as an Egyptian ruler, speaking roughly, he looked like every other Egyptian in the land.

precepts.text: Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for Joseph had straitly sworn the children of Israel to carry his bones away with them.
precepts.point: That is why no Egyptologist can show you the mummy of Joseph, the tomb of so famous a man: when Israel fled out of the land of Egypt they took the bones of Joseph with them, according to that oath.

note.label: Genesis 50: The Burial of Jacob and the Forgiveness of Joseph

precepts.why:
Joseph took an oath of the children of Israel before he died: “God will surely visit you, and ye shall carry up my bones from hence.” They embalmed him and “he was put in a coffin in Egypt.” Exodus shows that oath being kept. When Israel went out of Egypt, “Moses took the bones of Joseph with him: for he had straitly sworn the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you; and ye shall carry up my bones away hence with you.”

That is why no Egyptologist can show you the mummy of Joseph, the tomb of so famous a man. Joseph lived an hundred and ten years in Egypt, saw Ephraim’s children of the third generation and had the children of Machir the son of Manasseh brought up upon his knees, yet his body is not in Egypt. When Israel fled out of the land they took the bones of Joseph with them, according to that oath.

precepts.text: The Canaanites saw the mourning and called it a grievous mourning to the Egyptians; Jacob's family blended in with the Egyptians among them.
precepts.point: The difference was made plain in the plague itself: the houses whose firstborn died were shown not to be his people.

note.label: Exodus 11: The Death of the Firstborn Announced

precepts.why:
At Jacob's funeral the Canaanites saw the mourning in the floor of Atad, and “they said, This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians: wherefore the name of it was called Abel–mizraim”. The mourners were the family of Jacob, but the Canaanites called them Egyptians, because no one could tell the difference. Jacob's family blended in with the Egyptians among them.

Moses, Paul, Joseph with his own brothers, and Jacob's family at his funeral: over and over Israel was taken for Egyptians. That is why the Lord said “that ye may know how that the Lord doth put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel.” The difference was made plain in the plague: the houses whose firstborn died were shown not to be his people, and the houses where not a dog moved his tongue were Israel.

precepts.text: The nations thought evil against us, but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass as it is this day to save much people alive.
precepts.point: I will greatly praise the Lord with my mouth and praise Him among the multitude, for He shall stand at the right hand of the poor, the Israelites, to save him from those that condemn his soul. He saves the poor by His commandments; keeping God's commandments and enduring in this truth is how we will be saved.

note.label: Psalm 109: Give Myself unto Prayer

precepts.why:
“Let them curse, but bless thou: when they arise, let them be ashamed; but let thy servant rejoice.” Joseph said it to his brothers: “as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.”

The nations meant evil against us, but God means it for good, to bring to pass as it is this day, to save much people alive. So the adversaries are clothed with shame and covered with their own confusion, and the servant rejoices. He stands at the right hand of the poor, the Israelites, and saves them by his commandments; keeping God's commandments and enduring in this truth is how we will be saved.
